consensus_summary: Covenant primarily denotes a divinely initiated solemn binding relationship or commitment between God and his people, ratified by blood or signs, structuring redemptive history and fulfilled in the new covenant in Christ.
book_summary: Covenant is the binding word by which a head establishes and governs a relationship through law, promises, and judgments; parties come under the head’s terms rather than negotiating as equals, and God expressly calls the Ten Commandments his covenant.
consensus_core_identification: divinely initiated solemn binding relationship/commitment between God and people
book_core_identification: binding word of a head that establishes and governs a relationship through law, promises, and judgments
boundary_disagreement: Book excludes negotiated-contract or autonomous-equals models and centers the hierarchical word (explicitly identifying the Decalogue as the covenant); consensus primary keeps the broader relationship while treating treaty/contract forms only as alternatives.
rationale: Both locate the same biblical divine-human arrangement; the book preserves that category but materially tightens the identification from ‘relationship/agreement’ to the head’s governing word, reclassifying contractual-equals readings as obscuring and elevating the commandments-as-covenant texts. This is boundary/precision disagreement, not replacement of the referent.
strongest_objection: Consensus consistently treats the relationship itself as primary while the book relocates the essence to the word that creates it, which some may regard as shifting the referent rather than merely narrowing it.
